https://www.advanced-television.com/2026.text: Deutsche Telekom to acquire Fiberhost and Inea August 18, 2026 Deutsche Telekom has agreed to acquire 100 per cent of Fiberhost, a Polish open-access fixed network operator, together with Inea, a retail broadband and TV provider, for an enterprise valuation of c.€1 billion from current shareholders: Macquarie European Infrastructure Fund 5, a fund managed by Macquarie Asset Management and minority shareholders. The acquisition will accelerate T-Mobile Polska’s growth by adding Inea’s over 300,000 customers and Fiberhost’s fiber network passing over 1.4 million homes. The transaction marks a new step in T-Mobile Polska’s transformation from a mobile only operator into a fully convergent telecommunication provider. Since signing its first wholesale access agreement in 2018, T-Mobile has expanded its fixed coverage through wholesale partners and built a nationwide convergent offer. Together, the businesses will be better positioned to offer a high-quality convergent proposition and compete more effectively with operators that already own substantial fixed infrastructure to the benefit of Polish customers. The acquisition also strengthens T-Mobile Polska’s role as an investor in critical infrastructure supporting Poland’s digitalisation. Dominique Leroy, CEO Europe, Deutsche Telekom AG, commented: “This is an important milestone in T-Mobile Polska’s continuous growth story. By bringing together strong mobile and fibre capabilities, we are creating an even better foundation for simple, reliable services for our customers. At the same time, it will allow T-Mobile Polska to extend its contribution to the digitalistion of Poland and its economy. Investments like this matter beyond one market. Strong digital infrastructure is essential for Europe’s competitiveness, resilience and future growth. I am proud that Deutsche Telekom continues to play an active role in making that happen.” T-Mobile Polska CEO Andreas Maierhofer added: “We are opening a new chapter in T-Mobile Polska’s journey. Our award-winning mobile network, nationwide backbone, data centers and fibre infrastructure will now be complemented by our own fibre-to-the-home network reaching 1.4 million households. Owning an FTTH network will allow us to further develop our already successful portfolio of convergent products. Technological excellence, combined with our strong customer service – our key differentiators in the market – will strengthen our operations in Poland and help us build an even more attractive, quality-driven portfolio for both business and private customers at greater scale.” Cord Von Lewinski, Managing Director at Macquarie Asset Management, said: “Poland has been an important market for Macquarie for more than 20 years, from the development of the deepwater container terminal in Gdańsk through to Fiberhost and INEA. Over the past eight years we have partnered with management to support the development of Fiberhost and INEA, helping to create one of Poland’s leading fibre infrastructure platforms. Together, we expanded network coverage, increased wholesale access, and improved connectivity for communities and businesses across the country. We thank both management teams for their partnership and look forward to seeing both businesses continue to build on this strong foundation under Deutsche Telekom’s stewardship. We are proud to have supported development of important infrastructure, helping to drive Polish economic growth and positive societal impact.” Fiberhost will continue to offer transparent and non-discriminatory access to its state-of-the-art fibre infrastructure to all existing and potential internet service providers in Poland. Closing of the transaction is conditional upon customary Polish competition approvals. https://english.radio.cz/no-funding-rpi-.text: CS DE EN ES FR РУ УК No funding for RPI in draft 2027 budget but ministry says money may be found Facebook Twitter The Czech Republic’s draft state budget for 2027 does not include any funding for Radio Prague International, the news outlet Seznam Zprávy reported on Tuesday. In a chapter outlining the specific budget of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, which funds the station, no money is allocated for international radio broadcasting. The minister of foreign affairs, Petr Macinka, cut Radio Prague International’s budget by one-quarter this year and had said it would not receive any state backing in 2027. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs later told Seznam Zprávy that it had based its calculations on an expected change in the law – and if this legislation was not enacted by the end of 2026 it would cover expenditures for international broadcasting. The legal change evidently refers to an overhaul of the financing of public broadcasters. Meanwhile, a spokesperson for Czech Radio, of which RPI is part, said that the station was confident it would be able to reverse the plan to cut funding, and that talks on the matter were at an early stage. Photograph: Michael Nigro/Pacific Press/LightRocket/Getty Images Dakota Access pipeline Activists and leaders reflect on Standing Rock a decade on: ‘I would do it again’ Tribal leaders and organizers return to reservation 10 years after demonstrations against Dakota Access pipeline Sophie Sullivan in Standing Rock Tue 22 Sep 2026 11.17 EDT Last modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 11.19 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Ten years after major demonstrations against the Dakota Access pipeline , tribal leaders and Native American organizers returned to the Standing Rock Sioux reservation this week to honor the movement and its lasting impacts. In the rural reservation area of Fort Yates, a four-day encampment that centered on the phrase “mní wičóni” – “water is life” – brought together about 150 tribal members and allies for meals, drum circles, sacred ceremonies and memorials. It opened with the lighting of a sacred fire – “peta waken” – using coals preserved from a fire that burned at the 2016 camp. The tradition is a significant spiritual unification between the seven councils of the Oceti Sakowin, or Sioux Nation, tribes, typically done in times of historic and political efforts as a symbol of hope. In November 2016, after nearly two centuries had passed without the ceremony, Sioux tribal elders called for the fire to be relit after protesters – concerned that the Dakota Access pipeline (DAPL), which would run within a mile of tribal lands, might pollute the Standing Rock reservation’s water supply and encroach on Native lands and burial grounds – were maced , attacked by dogs and arrested en masse . View image in fullscreen Police use a water cannon on protesters during a protest near Cannon Ball, North Dakota, in November 2016. Photograph: Stephanie Keith/Reuters Later that winter, thousands more protesters or “water protectors” convened on the Great Plains, and outrage over the pipeline’s construction became a louder, global movement for Native rights and climate justice. But it did not stop Dallas-based Energy Transfer Partners from building the project, and national guard and police cleared the last holdout of protesters in an early 2017 military-style takeover . The pipeline now transports up to 750,000 barrels of oil a day from North Dakota to an Illinois refinery. In a powerful moment Thursday evening, Manape LaMere – an original headsman from the 2016 council and a member of the Sioux nation – retrieved the original coals and lit the fire as he had 10 years ago. One of LaMere’s other responsibilities at the Mni Wiconi gathering was to help perform a spiritual healing ceremony to help those who were at the camps find closure from the trauma of what they experienced. “When we sacrifice in camp the way we did, all that hardship and all that beauty, I always encourage people to call their spirit back,” LaMere said. “But because we got evicted the way we did, a lot of us may not have received that message, and I’ve seen people struggle.” Reunion attendees, at open mic sessions or around fire pits, reflected on how the often-violent standoffs between protesters and law enforcement in 2016 left many with lingering trauma, like for Candi Brings Plenty, a member of the Oglala Lakota Sioux nation. But, Brings Plenty said, while the event left scars, the community formed among camps has created lifelong strength. “I got the best knowledge and woksape, which is a Lakota word for wisdom, being at Standing Rock. I got so much empowerment and even though I got the worst-of-the-worst PTSD and everything that came along with it, you know, I would do it again,” Brings Plenty said. View image in fullscreen Activists sit around a campfire as it snows on the edge of the Standing Rock Sioux Reservation in December 2016. TSON/AFP/Getty Images Photograph: Jim Watson/AFP/Getty Images At the Prairie Knights Casino, the inaugural People of the Sun event brought together renewable energy groups, activists and performers for a three-day summit focusing on clean energy solutions. Speakers and panelists said that the protests 10 years ago underscored the need for Native reservations to build more sustainable energy systems that align with tribal values. One group making those systems a reality is the Sage Development Authority, a federally chartered corporation formed by the Standing Rock Sioux nation. The group uses grant funding to build wind farms for tribal district buildings, which allows local leaders to then reinvest that money back into their communities. Joseph McNeil, the CEO of SAGE and an enrolled member of the Standing Rock Sioux nation, said building infrastructure that allows his community to gain energy independence has intergenerational impacts. “The intergenerational poverty has been so dire, and being forced and your economy purposely depressed has been so intentional, that we can be voices for that and try to think of ways to help folks who aren’t there,” McNeil said. “We’re putting the stuff onto the district buildings, but it’s up to the district. We’re not going to dictate you, have your own choices, make your own decisions, and then live with those.” In support of the People of the Sun event was the actor Shailene Woodley, whose arrest at the protest 10 years ago spurred additional public discourse around the pipeline. “Do your research. Learn about the history, the real history of what happened to this country when our ancestors chose to colonize this land. And not from a place of guilt, not from a place of shame, but from a place of empowerment,” Woodley said in an interview. “If we don’t pay attention and if we don’t educate ourselves on what happened, then we’re going to continue to even unknowingly repeat those patterns and feed into the same cycles.” Explore more on these topics Dakota Access pipeline North Dakota Native Americans Protest (US) news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

Photograph: Ben Stansall/AFP/Getty Images Manston asylum centre Overcrowding and racism at Manston asylum centre linked to government decisions, inquiry hears Kent facility became dangerously overburdened after ministers halted transfers to hotels Diane Taylor Fri 25 Sep 2026 14.15 EDT Last modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 14.43 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A catalogue of failures including racism, use of force and chronic overcrowding at a Home Office processing site for people who arrive on small boat were linked to decisions made at the highest level of government, an independent inquiry has heard. The government commissioned the Manston independent inquiry to look at problems under the Conservative government between 1 June and 22 November 2022 at the facility in Kent. Almost 200 asylum seekers detained at Manston are participating in the inquiry along with the former home secretaries Suella Braverman and Priti Patel, several government departments including the Home Office, Treasury, Ministry of Justice and Ministry of Defence, and HM Inspectorate of Prisons and the UK Health Security Agency. The problems began when the site became vastly overcrowded. Manston was designed to hold a maximum of 1,600 new arrivals for no more than 24 hours as there are no proper sleeping or other facilities there. But after decisions by ministers to pause transfers of many of the asylum seekers to other accommodation such as hotels the site became dangerously overcrowded. Up to 4,000 people were accommodated there unlawfully for several weeks at the peak of the crisis, most of them sleeping on the floor in profoundly insanitary conditions. There were outbreaks of infectious conditions including scabies and diphtheria, the latter of which can be fatal in approximately 30% of cases in unvaccinated populations. There were also reports of assaults and drug use by guards, racist abuse from guards, and the death of a man after contracting diphtheria. The inquiry, chaired by Sophie Cartwright KC, heard that two former prime ministers, Boris Johnson and Rishi Sunak, who were both in post at different points in 2022, were involved in decision-making about the Manston site. Laura Dubinsky KC, representing some of the participants, told the inquiry that the decision to pause sending many asylum seekers on to hotels was in line with the thinking at No 10. “No 10 clearly did play a decision-making role,” she said. Patel has provided evidence to the inquiry that funding was deemed inadequate to address the small boats issue, including funding for Manston and onward accommodation. The inquiry heard that events in Manston “raise very serious questions for ministers”. Clair Dobbin KC, counsel to the inquiry, said it was taking place in a “crucible of hostility” at a time when the arrival of small boats remains a significant issue. She added that “to put it bluntly” the inquiry would look at whether at certain points “the entire operation at Manston was outside the law”. One senior Home Office official wrote a report saying: “To be frank, I’m struggling for words,” after observing what he said were “the worst conditions I have observed working in this environment”. Hussein Haseeb Ahmed, 31, was taken to Manston after arriving in a small boat. He died in hospital after becoming ill with diphtheria . He was belatedly admitted for care and was kept in handcuffs as he lay dying. The handcuffs were only removed two and a half hours before he died. According to the inquiry, evidence about his death suggests “a succession of missed opportunities”. The inquiry also heard that “very racist language was used towards detainees by some staff”. Sixty families were crammed into 11 rooms in a barracks building with no hot water, showers or clean clothes for nine days with one toilet for 81 people, and no soap or sanitiser available. Some used toothpaste to soothe bites and one used a croissant wrapper to dress wounds. Questions were raised about whether some unvetted staff were working legally at Manston. Shu Shin Luh, one of the lawyers representing participants in the inquiry, said: “Why were people treated as less than human?” Stephanie Harrison, also representing some of the participants in the inquiry, accused the Home Office of presiding over “an institutional culture defined by impunity with widespread illegality and non-compliance with the law”. Future dates for inquiry hearings have not yet been confirmed.
